title: Occasion
short: Written in October 1816 after a night reading George Chapman's Homer with Charles Cowden Clarke.
body: Clarke borrowed a copy of Chapman's folio Homer and he and Keats read it through the night, Keats shouting at passages of special energy. Clarke recalled that Keats walked home at dawn and that a copy of the sonnet was on Clarke's breakfast table by ten o'clock. It was printed in Leigh Hunt's Examiner on 1 December 1816 (in the article 'Young Poets') and in Keats's Poems (1817). Keats knew little Greek and had read Homer chiefly in Pope's smooth couplets; Chapman's vigorous Elizabethan version (Iliad 1598-1611, Odyssey 1614-15) came as a revelation.

title: Petrarchan sonnet and volta
short: An Italian sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd) whose sestet turns from reading to the similes of discovery.
body: The octave narrates the speaker's wide reading as travel and his failure to 'breathe' Homer's air until he heard Chapman; the volta at 'Then' (l. 9) turns to two similes for the shock of discovery, astronomical and geographical. The sestet rhymes cdcdcd. The final line, delayed by the dash and the run-on from l. 13, places the climactic word 'Silent' at the start of the line.

title: realms of gold
short: The world of great literature imagined as golden lands explored by a traveller.
body: The extended metaphor compares reading to voyaging through rich kingdoms, like the El Dorado sought by Renaissance explorers; it anticipates the explorer simile at the end. 'Goodly states and kingdoms' and 'western islands' continue the conceit, with a Spenserian colouring in 'goodly'. RPO notes that Keats read Homer only in translation, so these realms are the literature of the English and modern tradition.

title: western islands ... fealty to Apollo
short: Probably the poetry of Britain and western Europe, held by poets as feudal vassals of Apollo, god of poetry.
body: The 'western islands' are usually read as the literature of Britain (and perhaps the West generally), as opposed to the Greek East. 'Fealty' is the feudal oath of loyalty owed by a vassal to his lord; the bards hold their islands as fiefs from Apollo, god of poetry. The medieval-feudal vocabulary continues in 'demesne' (l. 6). Reading is thus figured as a tour of feudal territories, each held by a poet under the overlordship of the god of song, a playful conceit that suits a young poet's sense of a vast inherited literature.

title: deep-brow'd Homer ... demesne
greek: Old French demeine, Latin dominicus, 'belonging to a lord'
short: Homer, imagined as a thoughtful, heavy-browed ruler, holds the vast expanse as his own estate.
body: 'Demesne' is the land a lord keeps in his own possession. 'Deep-brow'd' suggests profound thought; Keats's earlier reading was 'low-brow'd', changed for the 1817 volume. The 'wide expanse' of Homer's poetry is something the speaker had only been told of, a contrast between report and experience. The legal and feudal vocabulary (fealty, demesne) extends the conceit of literature as a map of kingdoms, with Homer as the greatest of the lords, whose territory the speaker has only heard described by others, perhaps by Pope's translation.

title: pure serene
short: 'Serene' as a noun: a clear, calm expanse of air or sky.
body: The noun 'serene' (OED: a clear expanse of air or sky) was a poetic usage. RPO notes the phrase 'pure serene' in Coleridge's 'Hymn before Sun-rise, in the Vale of Chamouni' and in Cary's translation of Dante's Paradiso (XV). In the Examiner version the line read 'Yet could I never judge what men could mean'; the revision for the 1817 volume substituted the image of breathing Homer's air.

title: Chapman
short: George Chapman (c. 1559-1634), poet and dramatist, whose translations of Homer Keats read in 1816.
body: Chapman's Iliad, in fourteen-syllable lines, and Odyssey, in heroic couplets, are rugged, energetic and often free. 'Speak out loud and bold' praises their vigour in contrast to the polished Pope. Clarke recalled Keats's delight at the shipwreck of Odysseus in Odyssey V, where the sea had soaked his heart through. Keats's verb 'heard' is apt: they read aloud. Chapman's version later influenced other Romantic readers, and Keats's sonnet did much to revive his reputation.

sources.cite: Charles and Mary Cowden Clarke, Recollections of Writers (London, 1878), chapter on Keats

George Chapman, trans., The Whole Works of Homer (1616)

title: watcher of the skies ... new planet
short: Probably recalls William Herschel's discovery of Uranus in 1781, the first planet found since antiquity.
body: An astronomer who sees an unknown planet enter his field of vision. The discovery of Uranus by Herschel in 1781 was the obvious instance and is cited by RPO, though Keats need not have had a particular astronomer in mind. Keats had read about astronomy in Bonnycastle's Introduction to Astronomy, a copy of which he was given in 1811. 'Swims into his ken' is a gentle, fluid image of the planet entering sight.

title: ken
body: 'Ken' as a noun means the range of vision, and figuratively the range of knowledge or understanding (OED). The word joins the two kinds of discovery in the sestet: optical (seeing the planet) and intellectual (knowing Homer). It is a characteristically Scots and archaic word in English verse of the period, giving the line an elevated, slightly antique colour. The verb 'swims' suggests both the slow apparent movement of a planet across the field of a telescope and the dizziness of discovery, an effect that carries over into the next simile.

title: stout Cortez
short: A historical slip: Balboa, not Cortes, first saw the Pacific from Darien, in 1513.
body: Vasco Nunez de Balboa was the first European to see the Pacific, from a peak on the Isthmus of Darien in September 1513. Hernan Cortes, conqueror of Mexico, did not. Keats had been reading William Robertson's History of America, which describes both Balboa's view of the South Sea and Cortes's first view of Mexico, and probably conflated them. Readers have long pointed out the error; some critics argue it does not matter, or that Cortes's later, belated arrival fits Keats's belated discovery of Homer. 'Stout' means bold and strong.

title: wild surmise
short: An amazed conjecture: the men silently guess at what this vast ocean means.
body: 'Surmise' is a conjecture or suspicion. The men look at each other rather than at the sea, sharing a speechless astonishment; the shift of gaze from the eagle-eyed leader to his followers' faces is one of the sonnet's finest effects. Their silence corresponds to the speaker's own awe. 'Wild' suggests both untamed excitement and a guess that runs beyond evidence. The line thus registers both wonder and uncertainty about what lies ahead, which suits the speaker's sense of a newly opened world of reading.

anchor: Silent, upon a peak in Darien
title: Darien
short: The Isthmus of Darien, in present-day eastern Panama, between the Caribbean and the Pacific.
body: Darien is the region of the Panama isthmus from which Balboa first saw the Pacific. The sonnet ends with the word, and the position of 'Silent' at the start of the line gives the climax a hush. The phrase 'a peak in Darien' became proverbial for a moment of overwhelming discovery (Frances Power Cobbe used it in the title of a book in 1882).
